paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Babies, it seems, are born with musical preferences. At four months of age, dissonant (or harsh) notes at the end of a melody will cause them to squirm and turn away. If they like a particular tune, they make a contented sound. Scientists cite such responses as evidence that certain rules for music are wired into the brain from the earliest age, and musicians violate them at the risk of displeasing their audience. Hard-rock groups obey many of the same rules of harmony that, for example, Johann Sebastian Bach and other composers of classical western music followed in the 18th century. ‘Music is in our genes,’ says Mark Jude Tramo, musician and neuroscientist at the Harvard University Medical School in the US. ‘Many researchers like myself are trying to understand melody, harmony, rhythm, and the feelings they produce at the level of individual brain cells. At this level, there may be a universal set of rules that governs how a limited number of sounds can be combined in an infinite number of ways.’

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: ‘All humans come into the world with an innate capability for music,’ agrees Kay Shelemay, professor of music at Harvard University. ‘At a very early age, this capability is shaped by the music system of the culture in which a child is raised. That culture affects the construction of instruments, the way people sound when they sing, and even the way they hear sound. By linking research on what goes on in the brain with a cultural understanding of music, I expect we will learn a lot more than we would from either research emphasis alone.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The human brain is divided into two hemispheres, the right hemisphere being traditionally identified as the seat of music appreciation. However, studies of musical understanding in people who have damage to either hemisphere, as well as brain scans conducted while people listen to music, reveal that music perception emerges from the interplay of activity in both hemispheres. Some brain circuits respond specifically to music, but parts of these circuits are involved in other forms of sound processing. For example, the region of the brain dedicated to perfect pitch (the ability to perceive and name a particular musical note) is also involved in language perception. The front part of the brain (the frontal cortex) plays a role in rhythm and melody perception. ‘It is not clear what, if any, part these hearing centres play in "feeling" music,’ Tramo notes. ‘Other parts of the brain deal with emotion and pleasure. There is a good deal of effort going on to map connections between the parts of the brain involved with musical perception and the parts that participate in emotion.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Scientists have found activity in brain regions that control movement, even when people just listen to music without actually moving any parts of their bodies. In controlled experiments in research centres, as subjects imagined they were tapping out a rhythm, parts of their brain controlling body movement lit up on monitoring instruments. Music, it would seem, is as inherently motor as it is auditory. Many people pretend to ‘conduct’ while listening to classical music, hum along with familiar tunes, or dance to popular music. Add the contributions of facial expressions, stage lights and emotions, and you appreciate the complexity of what our brains put together while we listen to music in a concert.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Understanding the relationship between biology and music could allow people to use it better in medical and other beneficial applications beyond entertainment. There are already cases where music is exploited in this way. For example, some hospitals play soft background music in units for premature babies. Researchers have found that such music, as well as a nurse’s or mother’s humming, helps babies to gain weight faster and to leave the unit earlier than those not exposed to these sounds. Scientists have also found that music may lower blood pressure and increase the efficiency of oxygen consumption by the heart. One study showed that the heart muscle of people running on a treadmill did not work as hard when people listened to music as it did when they ran in silence. Then there are stories, in many cases undocumented scientifically, about athletes using music to enhance their performance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Music and the dancing that often accompanies it has been important to humans through the ages and all over the world. Some scientists believe that music even preceded language acquisition in humans. Archaeologists have discovered flutes carved from animal bone by Neanderthals, a humanlike species who lived more than 50,000 years ago. No human community is known that does not have music, even those people who live in relative isolation from what is usually considered the technologically advanced world. Often music is a defining characteristic of a particular culture. Despite this, large gaps exist in our knowledge about the underlying biology of music. For example, we don’t know how the brain decides if music is consonant or dissonant. Neither do we know whether the practice of music helps people master other skills, such as mathematics, or interpret the visual representation of information in pictures or diagrams.

groups.title: Music through the ages
content: Scientists believe that music and dancing may have been created by ancient humans even before they developed {{24}} . Remains of musical instruments made of bone indicate such early development. Different societies today, even those living in comparative {{25}} , have some form of music, and that music is often regarded as an important social element.

However, we know very little about the biology underlying music. We have not proved that music practice can aid in the improvement of other abilities like {{26}} , or in the interpretation of pictures and diagrams.
